name: Camel milk

card.summary: A traditional milk used in some regions as a food and in skincare products, with producers pitching it as a gentle, nourishing ingredient for skin.
card.note: Raw camel milk can carry infections such as brucellosis and MERS-CoV risk is documented in camel contact.

quick.overview:
Camel milk is a staple of desert herding cultures and is now sold as a dairy alternative and in some skincare products, for example by Australian camel dairies.

The appearance payoff people look for is nourished, moisturised skin. Published trials of drinking camel milk have focused on conditions such as asthma, autism and diabetes rather than skin appearance.
quick.how: It is drunk, or applied in lotions and soaps containing it. Fermented versions such as shubat and leben are traditional.
quick.risks: Reviews document zoonotic diseases linked to camels, including brucellosis and MERS-CoV, so raw milk carries infection risk.[2] Camel dairying is costly and retail milk can be many times the price of cow milk.[1]

lead: Camel milk is milk from dromedary and Bactrian camels, a staple for desert nomadic cultures and a growing niche product elsewhere.[1] It tastes similar to cow milk but slightly saltier, and fat content is reported at roughly 1-6 percent depending on source.[1]
Some Australian camel dairies also produce skincare products, and camel milk appears in the skincare space as a traditional remedy.[1]

chain: Camel milk applied topically or in cosmetics
angle.text: Producers and traditional users describe camel milk as nourishing for skin; published clinical trials of the milk examine other conditions.

paras: Global production was 2.85 million tonnes in 2017, with Somalia and Kenya supplying 64 percent.[1] Australia's camel dairy industry grew from 50,000 litres in 2016 to 180,000 litres in 2019.[1]
A review of camel-linked zoonoses found evidence of transmission to humans for MERS, brucellosis, plague, camelpox, hepatitis E and anthrax.[2]
No studies found on skin appearance. Randomised trials of drinking camel milk have examined asthma in children,[3] autism[4] and type 1 diabetes.[5]
